![](careing-for-data_banner.jpg){fig-alt="Abstract blue waves" width="100%"}

Research data in the humanities and social sciences is rarely simply "open" or "closed". Much of
it describes people — their words, their images, their suffering — and asking what it means to
*care* for such data is a question of ethics as much as of infrastructure. The **CARE
principles** put collective benefit, authority to control, responsibility and ethics beside the
FAIR ones, and this workshop asks what that looks like in practice.

For the seventh edition of "… in Dialogue", researchers bring concrete datasets to the table and
discuss how they handle the ethical questions each one raises. Short pitches are combined with hands-on work and with perspectives from law
and information security.

**9 December 2026 · Dome Room (Kuppelraum), Main Building (H4), University of Bern · the event is held in English.**

Short link to this page: <https://bit.ly/imdialog2026>

## Abstracts

Abstracts are published here as they are confirmed. The Data Stewards' pitch, Elisa Fornalé's
pitch and the "Bring your own data" session are still to come.

::: {.disclosure-list}

<details>
<summary><span class="d-title">Beyond FAIR: CARE, Community Responsibility, and the Challenges of (Historical) Sociolinguistic Data</span><span class="d-who">Anita Auer · keynote</span></summary>

(Historical) Sociolinguistic research presents a range of challenges concerning the
collection, representation, and ethical handling of linguistic data. While the FAIR
principles (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) provide guidelines for
research data management, the CARE principles (Collective Benefit, Authority to Control,
Responsibility, and Ethics) foreground questions of representation, ownership, and community
responsibility.

This talk explores the opportunities and tensions between these principles through two
sociolinguistic case studies. The first – historical sociolinguistic – case study examines
pauper letters from 1795-1834, highlighting challenges of archival regulations, questions of
copyright, and the creation of reusable historical corpora. The second focuses on Swiss
Heritage Tamil, where the question of responsible (meta) data sharing raises ethical
considerations. Drawing on practical experiences from both projects, I discuss data
collection, curation, as well as the ethical considerations that place limits on data
sharing. In particular, I highlight how commitments to CARE may conflict with expectations of
openness and reuse under FAIR, making certain data unsuitable for public access. Ultimately,
the talk asks how we can navigate these tensions while creating sociolinguistic datasets that
are both scientifically valuable and ethically responsible.

</details>

<details>
<summary><span class="d-title">The Case of Digital Scholarly Editing: How to Mediate Discrimination in Annemarie Schwarzenbach's Texts and Photographs</span><span class="d-who">Elias Zimmermann & Levyn Bürki</span></summary>

Once a corpus has been defined on the basis of scientific and legal considerations, scholarly
editions face less of a challenge in selecting which sensitive data to collect or display. Their
task might be to edit data that is ethically problematic but — sometimes precisely for that
reason — historically and philologically important. Our focus is therefore on the question of how
to mediate such material from the data level up to its display in the frontend.

Since 2025, the Schwarzenbach Edition (in particular Levyn Bürki, Daniela Kohler and Elias
Zimmermann) has developed its own discrimination-sensitive editorial guidelines in consultation
with postcolonial researchers and GLAM institutions. The guidelines set out fundamental
considerations regarding the presentation of content and translate them into specific policies for
tagging, annotation and presentation. For example, discriminatory expressions are marked up in
TEI/XML to enable the automated and targeted display of content notes with references to
explanatory editorial comments in the frontend. We argue that discrimination-sensitive editing
should not be viewed merely as a technical, presentational or philological challenge, but that all
three aspects should be considered in close conjunction with one another.

</details>

<details>
<summary><span class="d-title">Patient texts from German psychiatric hospitals of the 19th- and early 20th centuries</span><span class="d-who">Markus Schiegg</span></summary>

The Corpus of Historical Patient Documents (CoPaDocs) is based on texts written by patients from
19th- and early 20th-century psychiatric hospitals in Germany. Despite being over 100 years old,
consulting these sources means entering the realm of medical confidentiality. Their high
scientific relevance, however, justifies their archiving and use (Fichtner 1997: 116). This
presentation shows how CoPaDocs deals with this tension in practice. The sociolinguistic focus of
my research (see Schiegg 2022) contradicted with a full pseudonymisation, meaning that only a
patient's surnames was abbreviated to the first letter, and the first name, together with a large
amount contextual information relating to the individuals, has been published. However, access to
certain contextual data, in particular a patient's medical diagnosis, was made more difficult by
limiting the search options. They were designed to prevent quick searches within the illness
metadata and any resulting ahistorical or voyeuristic misuse.

**References**

- CoPaDocs = Schiegg, Markus (ed.) (2023): *Corpus of Patient Documents.*
  <https://deutschestextarchiv.github.io/copadocs/>;
  <https://www.dwds.de/d/korpora/copadocs>
- Fichtner, Gerhard (1997): Das Problem der Schweigepflicht und der Historiker. In: Dietrich Meyer
  & Bernd Hey (eds.): *Akten betreuter Personen als archivische Aufgabe. Beratungs- und
  Patientenakten im Spannungsfeld von Persönlichkeitsschutz und historischer Forschung.*
  Neustadt/Aisch: Degener, 111–122.
- Schiegg, Markus (2022): *Flexible Schreiber in der Sprachgeschichte. Intraindividuelle Variation
  in Patientenbriefen (1850–1936).* Heidelberg: Winter.

</details>

<details>
<summary><span class="d-title">Who CAREs about Witches?</span><span class="d-who">Christa Schneider</span></summary>

How much ethical responsibility do researchers have towards individuals who died centuries ago,
particularly when their personal histories are preserved in records of criminal prosecution?
Drawing on research with early modern witch-trial records from Switzerland and beyond, this talk
explores how the ethical treatment of historical data varies across national and institutional
contexts. While Swiss archival practices impose very little restrictions on working with these
records, access to e.g. comparable Scottish material has required ethical procedures similar to
those applied to contemporary court records. This contrast raises questions about the relevance of
anonymisation, the identifiability of historical individuals, and the extent to which contextual
information should be preserved or disclosed. Using concrete examples, the talk considers how the
CARE Principles might inform our responsibilities towards individuals represented in historical
records, even centuries after their deaths.

</details>

<details>
<summary><span class="d-title">Ethnographic Data: Between In-Depth Description and the Need to Protect Interlocutors</span><span class="d-who">Stefan Leins</span></summary>

As social anthropologists, we often generate ethnographic data through participation in other
people's everyday lives, work routines, and social situations. We also generate data through
interviews, as well as through informal conversations that are often not standardized and not even
recorded. The idea is that the closer we get to our interlocutors, the better we can portray their
lives and practices through what we call thick description. However, these data are often highly
personal and intimate. How can we navigate the discrepancy between our desire to provide detailed,
personal accounts and our responsibility to protect our interlocutors? This tension will be at the
center of my data pitch.

</details>

<details>
<summary><span class="d-title">Whose Data, Whose Benefit? The values behind CARE — and what they demand of the scientific community and of infrastructures like CLARIN</span><span class="d-who">Cristina Grisot</span></summary>

Language resources shared through infrastructures like CLARIN are usually judged by FAIR criteria
— Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable — but FAIR never asks who the data serves,
controls, or benefits. This talk turns to the CARE Principles for Indigenous Data Governance and
asks: what do CARE's underlying values — collective benefit, authority to control, responsibility,
ethics — demand of the scientific community, and of infrastructures like CLARIN, when the
community isn't Indigenous? Drawing on work done in the CLARIN community and Swiss dialectology
research, it proposes practical steps.

</details>

<details>
<summary><span class="d-title">A Safe Space for Testimony: CARE and the Research Infrastructure for Studying Sexual Abuse in the Environment of the Catholic Church in Switzerland</span><span class="d-who">Moritz Mähr & Magda Kaspar</span></summary>

The research project on the history of sexual abuse in the Catholic Church in Switzerland uses
highly sensitive data from church and state archives, as well as many interviews with affected
persons. These data are subject to strict data protection and privacy requirements and can
therefore be made accessible only with restrictions. At the same time, the research findings must
remain transparent and verifiable for other researchers. This contribution addresses this tension
and asks how the necessary protection of affected and accused persons can be reconciled with
scientific verifiability and long-term archiving.

</details>

<details>
<summary><span class="d-title">"There was a time when demons just did the trick." — CAREing for cultural property in the Information Age</span><span class="d-who">Sebastian Borkowski</span></summary>

Capitalism and colonial exploitation converted day-to-day objects of past societies into a
monetisable resource with unregulated profit margins and heralded nationalist and fascist coping
strategies for postcolonial identity crisis. By destroying the archaeological context, illicit
excavations of antiquities destroy the primary source of information about the ancient social and
cultural customs fossilised in archaeological objects. To prevent looting and the illicit trade in
antiquities, the location and dating of archaeological sites are treated as sensitive data by
governments and archaeologists. This secrecy conflicts with open research data policies and
ethical responsibilities for knowledge dissemination and public education — a debate that does not
necessarily involve the voices of descendant communities.

In the input presentation, I provide a short outline of the general problematic of illicit
excavations and current (best practice) solutions, before I turn the attention toward the current
state of negotiations about the reuse and open access publication of unpublished and published
archaeological data from Southern Iraq between the SNSF Sinergia project
[HyMes](https://hymes.ch) and the Iraqi State Board of Antiquities and Heritage.

</details>

<details>
<summary><span class="d-title">When Every Minute Identifies: Emergency Medicine Data at the Boundary of Openness</span><span class="d-who">Martin Müller</span></summary>

Emergency medicine depends on detailed information: exact times and locations, clinical
narratives, images, treatment sequences and information about relatives or witnesses. These
details are essential for accurate diagnosis and meaningful research, but they can also make
patients identifiable even after names have been removed. Using fictional cases and examples from
emergency medicine registries, this short talk examines which data are particularly sensitive, who
may be affected by their disclosure, and how public availability could lead to individual and
systemic harm — from violence, discrimination and coercion to loss of trust, delayed care and
biased research. It argues that valuable knowledge, metadata, code and aggregate findings should
be shared openly, while person-level emergency records require purpose-limited, secure and
accountable access.

</details>

<details>
<summary><span class="d-title">Learning to See the Problem: Discrimination-Sensitive Metadata in Practice</span><span class="d-who">Moritz Mähr · hands-on session</span></summary>

Metadata are not neutral: the ways in which historical sources and research data are described
shape what can be found, how people and events are represented, and which historical power
relations are reproduced. This hands-on session introduces the *Handbook for
Discrimination-Sensitive Metadata Practice*, which combines critical reflection on discrimination,
bias, representation, and power with practical guidance and checklists for working with metadata.
Participants will use these checklists to examine examples from their own institution, or an
institution of their choice, and identify potentially problematic descriptions, classifications,
omissions, and contextualisations. The aim is not to provide a simple checklist of "right" and
"wrong" terms, but to develop awareness of how discrimination can become embedded in metadata
practices and to strengthen participants' ability to recognise and critically discuss problematic
cases.

</details>

<details>
<summary><span class="d-title">Open, but Not at All Costs: Balancing Openness, Data Protection, and Ethical Responsibility in Research Data</span><span class="d-who">Gianfranco Valsecchi</span></summary>

What does it mean to share research data fairly and responsibly? It is now widely recognised that
research data should be as open as possible and as restricted as necessary, while legal and
ethical considerations may require additional safeguards and restrictions. Different degrees of
openness can help balance these two principles by allowing data to be shared and reused under
varying conditions, depending on the level of access provided and the types of reuse permitted,
while taking into account the legal, ethical, and social considerations at stake.

</details>

:::
